sp.rationale: I estimate the saw's feed velocity across the board, rather than the reciprocating blade velocity. Using the ruler's 1 cm graduations as an approximate image scale, the cutting traverse is roughly 22 cm. The frame grid shows the saw entering the cut around 6.4–7 s and reaching the far edge at about 17.1 s, giving approximately 22 cm / 10 s = 2.2 cm/s. sp.rationale: I estimate the net acceleration using coarse second differences of the astronaut’s image-center positions in the frame grid at 0, 0.42, and 0.83 s, which bracket 0.5 s. The approximate centers, expressed within each panel, are (49, 200), (80, 215), and (132, 215) pixels. Using the given 2.2 m height and an approximately 90-pixel astronaut height gives a scale of 0.024 m/pixel; the resulting horizontal and vertical acceleration components have magnitudes roughly 2.9 and 2.1 m/s², giving about 3.5 m/s² overall. This is a rough image-based estimate affected by changing pose and perspective. I do not use the strict read-out of 3076.5 m/s² because it is an unsupported derivative of an underdetermined pose table.

sp.reason: the measurement ganymede_orbital_diameter: no plane to back-project onto
sp.rationale: I estimated the scale directly from the overlays, assuming the nearly circular, concentric orbital paths lie in the same approximately image-parallel plane. Callisto moves through about 0.49 radians on an orbit of roughly 185 pixels radius over 3.30 seconds, giving an image-path length of about 91 pixels. Its given speed of 0.627 m/s implies a physical path length of 2.069 m and a scale of approximately 0.0227 m/pixel. The visible Ganymede orbital ring is about 241 pixels in diameter, giving approximately 5.5 m. This is a visual planar estimate rather than a determined program read-out, since the reconstruction does not establish Ganymede's orbital plane.

sp.rationale: I estimate about 0.2 m, assuming the soccer ball continues bouncing on the floor after it leaves view. The program summary places its second floor encounter near 1.21 s. Its first bounce implies a restitution coefficient of approximately 0.70, using the fitted incoming and outgoing vertical velocities and gravity. Applying that same coefficient to subsequent bounces gives a further floor contact around 1.85–1.9 s and a surface-to-floor clearance of roughly 0.2 m at 2.0 s. This is uncertain because those later bounces are unobserved; I did not use the unsupported negative height in the strict read-out.
